name: SNAP-8

lead: SNAP-8 (acetyl octapeptide-3) is a longer relative of Argireline used in serums and eye creams to soften expression lines on the forehead and around the eyes. It is often described as a stronger version of Argireline.

It is built on the same SNAP-25-derived sequence and is proposed to interfere with SNARE complex assembly, reducing neurotransmitter release at the muscle junction in a way conceptually similar to botulinum toxin but milder and reversible. A 2020 review reported no peer-reviewed clinical study of the peptide on its own and noted that the wrinkle-reduction figures in circulation come from the manufacturer.

paras: It is applied as a daily serum or eye cream, usually as one ingredient among several in anti-aging products, with changes judged over weeks. Injectable versions are discussed only on forums.
It is considered low risk and is unrestricted as a cosmetic ingredient. Reported effects are modest and reversible, and skin delivery is reported to limit its effect.

Can This Smoothing Serum Replace Botox Treatments?

angle.text: SNAP-8 is used in serums and eye creams to soften forehead and eye-area expression lines, and is described as a longer relative of Argireline. It imitates part of a muscle-signalling protein to reduce contraction slightly. Claims come mainly from manufacturer data, and independent human trials are scarce.

lead: SNAP-8, the trade name of acetyl octapeptide-3, is a synthetic peptide used as a topical cosmetic ingredient in serums, creams, eye products and dissolving microneedle patches marketed for expression lines, particularly on the forehead and around the eyes [1]. People use it as a daily, injection-free product with the aim of softening the lines that form where facial muscles repeatedly contract, so that the forehead and eye area look smoother.

It is described as an extended analogue of acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline), built on the same SNAP-25-derived sequence with additional amino acids at one end [1][2]. Like Argireline, it is proposed to compete with the protein SNAP-25 in assembling the SNARE complex, which would reduce neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction and so muscle contraction, in a manner conceptually similar to botulinum toxin but milder and reversible [1][2][3][4].

Published evidence specific to SNAP-8 is sparse. A 2020 review reported no peer-reviewed clinical study of the peptide on its own and noted that the wrinkle-reduction figures in circulation come from the manufacturer's website; the human studies that exist test it as one ingredient among several [2][5][6]. Reviews of cosmetic peptides generally describe a limited number of in vivo clinical trials for the category [7].

The entry covers the peptide's structure and proposed mechanism, its relationship to Argireline and botulinum toxin, the manufacturer data and independent studies, delivery questions such as skin penetration, safety and regulatory status, dermatologists' views, and how the ingredient appears in skincare and looksmaxxing discussion.
infobox: Acetyl octapeptide-3 (also listed as acetyl glutamyl heptapeptide-1) [1]
Cosmetic ingredient; not an approved drug
Very low final concentrations, reported as roughly 0.0015 to 0.005 percent active peptide [1]
Developed and sold by Lipotec, now part of Lubrizol (as described by Grokipedia) [1]

paras: SNAP-8 is a linear peptide with an acetylated N-terminus and amidated C-terminus. Its sequence contains that of Argireline plus an alanine-aspartate extension [1][2]. Descriptions in the literature use inconsistent names for it, including octapeptide and heptapeptide labels, and Argireline itself appears as both acetyl hexapeptide-3 and acetyl hexapeptide-8 in different reviews [2][7][3]. Grokipedia gives two slightly different molecular weights, about 1,073 and 1,075 g/mol, without reconciling them [1].

Proponents and manufacturers describe it as a competitive inhibitor of SNARE complex formation. A 2020 review reported that in an in vitro assay a 1.5 millimolar concentration inhibited release by about 43 percent, and that combining SNAP-8 with another peptide gave a larger effect than either alone in that assay (SNAP-8 alone 38 percent, a second peptide alone 7 percent, equal parts of both 47 percent) [2]. The review draws these figures from the manufacturer's literature and notes that its own nomenclature for the peptide is inconsistent [2].

The mechanism rests on the SNARE complex, the protein machinery that lets neurotransmitter vesicles fuse with the nerve ending and release acetylcholine. The core complex is a four-helix bundle to which synaptobrevin and syntaxin each contribute one helix and SNAP-25 contributes two [4]. Botulinum toxin type A is a protease that cleaves SNAP-25, whereas the cosmetic peptides are proposed to compete with it reversibly rather than cut it [1][4][8]. Grokipedia and the manufacturer literature describe the effect as occurring in the superficial skin, with lower potency than injected toxin [1].

sections.h: Relationship to Argireline and botulinum toxin
paras: Argireline, the shorter peptide on which SNAP-8 is modelled, is the better-studied of the two. Wikipedia attributes its description as an antiwrinkle peptide to a 2002 paper by Blanes-Mira and colleagues and says it has been sold as Argireline since 2001, now by Lubrizol [3]. It states that no dedicated double-blind clinical trial of its anti-wrinkle efficacy is currently available, that a 2025 review found improvement in some studies but inconsistent statistical significance, and that no study has compared it directly with botulinum toxin [3].

A 2025 review of skin-ageing peptides reports a 4-week randomised, double-blind trial of Argireline on periorbital wrinkles in Chinese subjects with 48.8 percent anti-wrinkle efficacy versus placebo, and a 30-day study of a 10 percent Argireline emulsion in which wrinkle depth fell by up to 30 percent; the same review gives no numerical efficacy results for acetyl octapeptide-3 and lists it at 0.05 percent in solution [7]. SNAP-8 is also reported in polymeric nanospheres as a possible alternative to botulinum toxin, without outcome data in that review [7].

Botulinum toxin is the reference point for all of these peptides. Wikipedia describes the FDA approval of Botox Cosmetic in 2002 for frown lines between the eyebrows, a smoothing effect typically visible within three to five days and lasting about two to four months, with side effects that mostly come from unintended paralysis of nearby facial muscles [8]. Neurotoxin injections are procedures given by clinicians, and the cosmetic peptides are positioned as a topical alternative that does not involve them.

SNAP-8 appears as a named ingredient in anti-ageing serums and eye creams, often marketed as an upgrade to Argireline, and is used on the forehead (frown and horizontal lines) and around the eyes (crow's feet) [1]. It is used consistently over weeks rather than producing an immediate effect, and its effect is described by suppliers as temporary and dependent on continued use [1]. Dissolving hyaluronic acid microneedle patches carrying the peptide are a newer delivery format intended to carry it past the outer skin layer [5][6].

Dermatologists quoted in consumer press describe peptide serums as most useful for people who prefer to avoid injectables or who want to maintain results between treatments, rather than as replacements for neurotoxin injections [9][10].

The best-known efficacy figures for SNAP-8 come from the manufacturer. A 2020 review cites Lipotec's website for a maximum wrinkle reduction of 62 percent and a mean of 35 percent, and states that it identifies no independent peer-reviewed clinical study of SNAP-8 [2]. Grokipedia reports a manufacturer test in 17 women using a solution delivering roughly 0.005 percent active peptide twice daily for 28 days, with a 34.98 percent reduction in wrinkle depth versus 27.05 percent for Argireline, and a separate unpublished claim of up to 72 percent; it describes independent clinical evidence as limited [1]. These figures are the manufacturer's and have not been independently replicated.

A recurring technical question is whether a peptide applied to the skin surface reaches the nerve endings it is proposed to act on. The 2025 review notes that poor membrane permeability is probably one of the most significant disadvantages of peptides, because the lipid-rich outer skin layer is a barrier to water-soluble peptides, and lists chemical enhancers, microneedles, iontophoresis, sonophoresis, radiofrequency and nanocarriers as delivery methods under study [7]. For Argireline, Wikipedia cites a 2015 study finding that under 0.2 percent of the peptide crossed the outer skin layer after 24 hours [3]. The 2020 review reports that microneedles increased Argireline permeation by up to about 40-fold compared with passive diffusion [2].
Grokipedia itself states that SNAP-8 penetrates shallowly, which it presents alongside the efficacy claims without reconciling the two [1].

A 2024 comparative study in Annals of Dermatology, by authors affiliated with the patch developer Raphas Co. in Seoul and the Catholic University of Korea, enrolled 24 adults aged 30 to 65 (21 completed) with eye wrinkles. Each person wore a dissolving hyaluronic acid microneedle patch containing SNAP-8 (0.03 percent) together with ascorbic acid glucoside and sodium cyclic lysophosphatidic acid on one eye, and a hyaluronic acid-only patch on the other, nightly for 14 days and then every third day to day 28. Several skin-roughness measures differed from placebo by day 28, transepidermal water loss fell on days 7 and 14, and the authors reported no adverse effects [5].

The authors attribute early effects to SNAP-8 and later effects mainly to the other ingredients; the study was small, the text does not clearly describe blinding or randomisation, penetration depth was measured in minipig skin, and several authors were employees of the patch manufacturer [5].

A 2020 single-centre clinical study examined hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several bioactive peptides for dermal tolerability and anti-ageing effect; as a multi-ingredient product, its results cannot be assigned to one peptide [6]. No published randomised trial has tested SNAP-8 alone against placebo or against botulinum toxin, according to the 2020 review of cosmeceutical peptides [2]. For the broader category, the 2025 review describes most bioactivity studies as in vitro and notes a significant shortage of in vivo clinical trials [7].

No adverse events beyond normal skin tolerance were reported in the small microneedle patch study [5]. Grokipedia describes the ingredient as having shallower skin penetration and lower potency than injected botulinum toxin and as free of the injection-related risks of that procedure [1]. Wikipedia reports that Argireline studies, including a pilot trial in blepharospasm patients, found no significant adverse effects [3]. No long-term or pregnancy safety data specific to SNAP-8 were identified.

Reviews of cosmetic peptides generally describe them as well tolerated topically, but note that detailed adverse-event reporting is limited, and a 2025 review gives no SNAP-8-specific safety data [7].

Grokipedia reports that SNAP-8 is listed in the EU's CosIng database as a humectant and skin conditioner, is not restricted under Annexes II or III of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, and needs no FDA pre-market approval for cosmetic use in the United States [1]. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than an approved drug, and Grokipedia says it is intended only for topical use, not injection [1].

SNAP-8 appears as a named ingredient in anti-ageing serums and eye creams, usually at very low final concentrations, and is often marketed alongside or as an upgrade to Argireline [1]. A 2024 Zoe Report feature on neuropeptide skincare quoted dermatologist Jeannette Graf saying such products are not nearly as effective as injectable neurotoxins; the article mentions SNAP-8 once, in the description of an eye product [10].

An Allure piece republished by Yahoo Style Canada in September 2024 reported dermatologist Omer Ibrahim saying that nothing is a suitable alternative to Botox, while describing a peptide serum as effective for people who want to avoid injectables, and Rachel Westbay estimating up to about 30 percent improvement in fine lines with consistent use over months; the serum named in that article contains acetyl hexapeptide-8 rather than SNAP-8 [9].

Wikipedia has no article on the compound (a search for SNAP-8 returns an unrelated nuclear power programme). On looksmax.org a member wrote a guide thread presenting it as a possible anti-ageing peptide, with sections on how it works, clinical trials and what it will not fix, and a plan to research an injectable version [11]. Other peptide-focused websites also discuss SNAP-8 alongside research peptides; the guide's injectable idea is the author's own plan, and the sources cited here describe only topical cosmetic use [1][11].

lore.intro: A single looksmax.org guide thread presents SNAP-8 as a possible anti-aging peptide, framed by its author with the question 'Anti Aging Hack? Cope? Wrinkle Preventor?'. In skincare circles it is discussed as one of several 'Botox-like' topical peptides [11][10].

timeline.event: Botulinum toxin (Oculinum/Botox), developed by Alan Scott, is FDA-approved for eye muscle disorders; Richard Clark describes the first cosmetic use for forehead wrinkles [8].
Argireline, the shorter SNAP-25-derived peptide, becomes commercially available [3].
Blanes-Mira and colleagues publish the antiwrinkle activity paper on Argireline; FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines [3][8].
A study reported by Wikipedia finds under 0.2 percent of Argireline crosses the outer skin layer in 24 hours [3].

Frontiers in Chemistry review of cosmeceutical peptides reports manufacturer wrinkle figures for SNAP-8 and no independent clinical study; a single-centre study tests multi-peptide microneedle patches [2][6].
Annals of Dermatology publishes a 21-completer split-face study of a SNAP-8 microneedle eye patch [5].
Biomolecules review of skin-ageing peptides lists acetyl octapeptide-3 without efficacy data [7].
